title: What should you eat for a better night’s sleep?
intro: Have you ever had the feeling of lying awake at night, unable to get to sleep? Many of us know what it is like to struggle with sleep, especially if we have drunk too much tea or coffee before bed! But did you know that your sleep quality can be affected by other parts of your diet too? Georgie and Phil discuss this and teach you some new vocabulary.
this_week_question: What percentage of people in the UK say they get less than seven hours sleep per night?
Listen to the programme to hear the answer.

vocab.desc: important substances that all lifeforms need to survive and be healthy saturated fats fats that are thought to be worse for our health, often found in meat and dairy deep sleep stage of the sleep cycle when the brain is at its slowest and the body can rest and repair supplements tablets and other consumables that contain particular  that you might not get in your everyday diet feed information give lots of information continuously magic bullet simple and effective solution, usually one that doesn't exist in reality

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Hi Georgie.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Hi Phil. Now, Phil, do you ever struggle to get a good night's sleep?

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: You know, I do sometimes. If I've been thinking about something a lot, or even worse, if I've had a cup of coffee later than I should, sometimes I can lie there for hours.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes. Well, many of us will be familiar with that feeling of lying in bed, feeling really tired, but just not being able to go to sleep, but what causes us to struggle to sleep and is there anything we can do about it? Well, researchers have for a while been interested in the link between what we eat and how we sleep. Today on 6 Minute English, we'll be talking about this and asking, "What should you eat for a better night's sleep?"

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: OK. Phil, let's start with a quiz question. So, adults need between 7–9 hours sleep a night to stay healthy, according to experts, but what percentage of people in the UK say they get less than this? Is it: a)    15%, b)    25%, or c)    35%?

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: OK. I think people find sleeping hard, so I think it's going to be c) 35%.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: OK. Well, we'll find out the answer later in the programme.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Georgie, you've been looking at the research on this. Do scientists think that what we eat affects how we sleep?

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes, they do. Scientists have done some long-term studies. So, looking at large groups of people over a long period of time, and they found that a healthier diet is associated with better quality sleep. They've also done some smaller studies looking in more detail at exactly what people are eating and then studying how they sleep in a laboratory.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: OK. And in these studies, have they found that particular foods are better for our sleep than others?

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, it's less about particular foods and more about particular nutrients . So, nutrients means important things your body needs to survive and be healthy. For example, protein is a nutrient . BBC World Service programme The Food Chain has been speaking to researcher Professor Marie-Pierre St-Onge about which nutrients are important for sleep.

transcript.author: Marie-Pierre St-Onge
transcript.text: So, diets that look more like a Mediterranean pattern – higher in fruits and vegetables, whole grains, lower in animal-based foods, lower in sugar. But then from our own research, where we evaluate food intakes in the lab, we see different... similar patterns, really. But when we talk about nutrients , diets that are higher in fibre, which we find in fruits and vegetables and whole grains, and lower in saturated fats , which we find in more plant-based types of foods, are associated with more deep sleep at night.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Marie-Pierre says that Mediterranean-style diets are associated with good sleep. A Mediterranean diet includes lots of vegetables and less animal-based foods such as meat and dairy.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Yes, and Marie-Pierre's own research shows that some nutrients , such as fibre, are important for sleep and others, such as saturated fats , are less important. Saturated fat is a type of fat mainly found in meat and dairy that's thought to be bad for your health.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Right. And according to Marie-Pierre, eating less saturated fat and more nutrients like fibre is associated with more deep sleep at night. A deep sleep is when you are more fully asleep and your body is able to rest.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: So, Georgie, it sounds like thinking about our diets is important if we want to improve our sleep. And now I've heard that certain foods have a lot of nutrients that can be helpful for sleep. Is that true?

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Well, there is some limited research on specific foods and their impact on sleep. So, for example, scientists have been studying kiwi fruits and also tart cherry juice. And you may also see adverts for supplements that claim to improve sleep. Supplements are tablets you take, which contain particular nutrients that you might not get in your everyday diet. But experts say that focusing on our whole diet, rather than one particular fruit or supplement , is going to be the most effective. Here's sleep doctor Allie Hare explaining more to BBC World Service programme The Food Chain.

transcript.author: Allie Hare
transcript.text: I think people are looking for the one supplement often or the... you know, we're fed a lot of these things, aren't we, on social media? This magical powder or this magical tablet that you can take that will, you know, help you sleep better immediately from tonight. And of course, you know, Marie-Pierre and I know that there is no such magic bullet , unfortunately. And if there was, I'm sure, you know, we would be... we would be doing very well for ourselves.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Allie says people are looking for a supplement that can help them sleep.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes. She says we are fed information on social media about magical tablets. If you are fed information , you are given lots of it in a continuous way.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: But Allie argues that experts know there's no magic bullet to help you sleep, and a magic bullet refers to a simple and effective solution to a problem that's usually one that doesn't exist. OK. Well, now I think it's time to find out the answer to your quiz question, Georgie.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: Yes. I asked you what percentage of UK adults say they get less than seven hours sleep a night.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: And I said I thought it was c) 35%.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: You are correct, Phil. Yes, 35% of adults say they get six hours or less sleep a night, according to a study by YouGov. OK. Let's recap the vocabulary we learned in this programme, starting with nutrients , which are important things your body needs to survive and be healthy.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Saturated fats are fats mainly found in meat and dairy products that are thought to be bad for our health.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: A deep sleep is when your body is fully asleep and able to rest.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: Supplements are tablets or other things which contain particular nutrients you might not get in your everyday diet.

transcript.author: Georgie
transcript.text: To feed information means to give lots of it in a continuous way.

transcript.author: Phil
transcript.text: And a magic bullet is a simple and effective solution, and it's often one that doesn't exist.

transcript.author: Georgie

transcript.author: Phil

transcript.author: Georgie
